newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's most wanted man says he will win vote.
newsitem.headline: Russia's most wanted man says he will win vote.

text.p: Guerrilla chief Shamil Basayev, Russia's most wanted man, forecast he would win breakaway Chechnya's presidential election on Monday.

Basayev, 32, heightened fears of a schism among Chechen guerrillas by taking a sharply critical line during the election campaign against his main rivals, who are all leading figures in the armed separatist movement.
But as he set off from his brick-built farmhouse home across a snowy field to vote in the mountain village of Vedeno, the man the Kremlin views as a "terrorist" took a more conciliatory tone.

Though saying he was sure of winning, Basayev told reporters he would "congratulate" any other victor and hoped for good relations with the other secessionist leaders, all of whom would be welcome to join his government.

Condemned in Moscow but hailed as hero in Chechnya for leading a bloody raid on the Russian town of Budennovsk in 1995, Basayev enjoys huge support around Vedeno, which was a centre of resistance during 21 months of war with Moscow.
Basayev held almost 1,000 people hostage in a hospital before eluding Russian commandos and slipping back into Chechnya. The raid helped change the course of the war.

Dozens of adoring Chechens, from excited young girls in demure headscarves to hobbling elders in shaggy sheepskin hats, greeted the quietly spoken black-bearded fighter at the polling station. Villagers built Basayev a new house after his previous one was blown up by Russian troops.
"I'm for Basayev, who else?" said 25-year-old Razet, her eyes smiling. "I've nothing against the others. But Basayev is a worthy man. He gave us our freedom."
"He's very fair. And he saved Chechnya from genocide," said Yusup Chigayev, 62, as he mounted his pony after voting and rode off into the brilliantly sunny mountain morning.

Basayev, wearing the grey city coat and fur hat in which he has campaigned after shedding his combat fatigues, pledged that his first task in office would be "to consolidate our independence as a state".
Unlike Aslan Maskhadov, the army commander who is the clear frontrunner in straw exit polls across, Basayev played down the need for international recognition.
"We don't need it that badly. We haven't yet recognised the world and the world hasn't suffered for it, has it?" he said with a flash of dry humour.
The unilateral independence, declared by late separatist leader Dzhokhar Dudayev in 1991 and defended during two years of bloody conflict, is "enough for us", he said.
Russia, on the other hand, needed to accept Chechnya's sovereignty as a fait accompli, he said. "It is to Russia's advantage to recognise us quickly and establish profitable relations with us."
Asked what would happen to Russia if it did not, Basayev, who previously threatened to extend the war to Russian soil, contented himself to replying: "It will fall apart."
Moscow's opposition to full Chechen independence is, in fact, based on the opposite view that to accept it would be to encourage other ethnic minorities to break away.
Whatever the argument, Basayev winning the Chechen presidency would be a nightmarish embarrassment for the Kremlin, which seems to much prefer the more moderately spoken Maskhadov.
